What this is. An Apply rep, like apply wss to venture. It takes the six problems from rodrigues derivatives problem map and tests them against the ten company studies summarized in cross company capability matrix.

The question. The company studies map the supply side: who sells pricing, risk systems, venues and clearing, and how they bought their way into each layer. The derivatives corpus maps the demand side: what problem each of those products solves, and why the problem is hard. Run together, does "which of the six problems does this firm carry or sell?" explain where the moats are, where the money is moving, and what gets bought next?

Provenance. Company figures are as each company states them, taken from the company notes cited inline. The six-problem frame comes from Rodrigues's posts. Lines marked (added context) are general market history from this note, not from either source. Like the company notes, the evidence is mostly each firm's own voice, so it shows what firms claim to solve, not independently measured share.

Maps to Course 04 (Competitive Strategy: moats), Exec E2 (Capital Allocation), E6 (Crisis), E10 (Digital & AI), Course 11 (Global Macro).

The six problems against the ten firms, in one table

Who sells the solution (venue, data or utility) versus who carries the problem on its own balance sheet. Firm abbreviations as in the capability matrix.

Problem Sold as Main sellers (matrix level 3) Who carries it Evidence

P2 Measure the risk Risk and portfolio platforms BLK (Aladdin), BBG (AIM/PORT) Funds, dealers Aladdin began as BlackRock's internal risk system (blackrock aladdin data); Goldman's SecDB in the 1990s (goldman markets platforms)
P3 Hedge it Venues, algos, dealer liquidity TW (rates), MKTX (credit), ICE (futures), GS/JPM (dealers) Corporates, funds, then dealers who take the other side TW SEF: $150tn, 52% of SEF volume in 2024 (tradeweb derivatives regulation)
P4 Will they pay Central clearing ICE (CDS), LSEG/LCH (swaps) Banks for bilateral trades; the CCP and its members for cleared ones ICE Clear Credit >80% of CDS clearing; SwapClear >90% of cleared IRS (ice clearing treasury, lseg post trade clearing)
P5 Fund it Financing, margin utilities, capital GS/JPM (financing), LSEG (Acadia) Dealers' balance sheets, then nonbanks Goldman financing: 19% of markets revenue (2018) → ~46% (Q3 2026) (goldman markets platforms)

Two firms appear on nearly every row: LSEG and ICE. They are the only two that sell both a P1 reference price and a P4 clearing house. The capability matrix calls them "near-complete stacks". In six-problem terms, they own the problem at the bottom (P1) and the one regulators made mandatory (P4).

Concept 1 · Whoever owns the reference price sits under everything else (P1)

The derivatives idea: every other problem uses P1 as an input. Risk (P2) is the change in a price; a hedge (P3) is sized off a price; CVA (P4) is a price adjustment; margin (P5) is called on a price move.

What the companies show: - ICE. Its fixed-income business earns $1,234M from data and analytics against $125M from execution (FY25, about 10:1). Best execution, TCA, liquidity scores, ICE indices and ICE's own venue all measure trades against ICE's evaluated price (ice fixed income data). - Bloomberg. Its position doesn't depend on venue share, which it never publishes. It depends on owning BVAL and then making protocols, indices and futures settle against it (bloomberg pricing bval ibval). - S&P is the exposed case. It sells pricing mainly as regulatory evidence (SEC Rule 2a-5), and part of its corporate-bond pricing rests on MarketAxess's CP+ feed, which ICE will own from 2027 (spglobal pricing fixed income). An evaluator that rents its prices has a weak P1 position. - A clearing house can make P1 decisions for the whole market. LCH moved to SOFR discounting in October 2020 across >1m contracts and $120tn notional (lseg post trade clearing). One discount-curve switch at a CCP re-valued a large part of the swaps market.

Verdict: this is the strongest fit. The firms with the highest-margin, stickiest businesses own a P1 price that other products are graded against. Execution is the cheaper layer on top.

Concept 2 · The risk system becomes the language (P2)

The derivatives idea: risk numbers are model-defined and fragile. Greeks are first-order approximations, vega isn't additive across expiries, and VaR is blind past its cutoff. Whatever system defines your risk numbers also defines what your desk is allowed to do.

What the companies show: Aladdin went from BlackRock's internal risk system to cloud SaaS, then to a portfolio workflow, a connectivity layer and a data business. Technology revenue roughly doubled from $785M (2018) to about $1.5B (2023) (blackrock aladdin data). The capability matrix names Aladdin "the control point": venues compete to be placed inside it (blackrock anchor client). Goldman took the same path from SecDB (firm-wide risk aggregation) to Marquee, which pushes its models to clients' desktops (goldman markets platforms).

Verdict: this fits, and explains why the switching costs are high. Changing risk platforms means changing the definitions your limits, reports and committees use. The derivatives lens adds the warning: the platform's risk numbers are only as good as its model choices, and clients rarely test them.

Concept 3 · Hedging moved to venues because regulation standardized it (P3)

The derivatives idea: a hedge only transfers risk cleanly if the instrument is standard and the other side is reliable. Custom hedges stay with dealers.

What the companies show: - Swaps. Tradeweb's swaps business was "made by regulation". Clearing mandates standardized swaps, trading mandates pushed them onto venues, and the LIBOR → SOFR switch forced the market to rebook positions through Tradeweb (tradeweb derivatives regulation). - Credit. MarketAxess's all-to-all pool rose from 27% (2019) to 35% of credit volume in March 2020, when dealers pulled back (marketaxess open trading). - Dealers. Goldman didn't fight electronification. It became broker, venue operator, principal and data distributor at once (goldman markets platforms).

What the derivatives corpus adds: the corporate hedge is still bespoke. His Brazil series shows a local dealer building synthetic onshore dollars to absorb an exporter's forward. No venue in the ten studies serves that client directly, and corporates appear in only 13 of his posts.

Verdict: this fits standardized hedges. It doesn't reach the corporate end-user, which is a gap in both sources.

Concept 4 · A clearing house is CVA, centralized (P4)

The derivatives idea: with a bilateral trade, each bank prices the other's default risk through CVA and holds capital against it. Central clearing replaces many bilateral exposures with one counterparty, the CCP, which nets them and backs them with margin and a default fund shared by its members.

What the companies show: - ICE. ICE Clear Credit was founded during the 2008 crisis and now claims >80% of CDS clearing, with a record $2.678tn cleared in a day (Mar 20 2026) (ice clearing treasury). The note's verdict is that "the moat is netting": one pool, one margin model, offsets "as high as 98%". - LCH. SwapClear has >90% of cleared interest-rate swap notional ($1,941trn in 2025). LSEG paid £1.15bn to buy back revenue it had shared with its dealer-members (lseg post trade clearing). - Clients push back on who bears losses. Goldman, BlackRock, JPMorgan and others co-wrote a 2019 paper asking CCPs to put more of their own capital first in line (goldman markets platforms).

Why netting creates winner-take-most: netting reduces both the exposure (the P4 cost) and the margin (the P5 cost). The bigger the pool, the more trades offset, the cheaper it is to clear there, and the more trades arrive. That is why ICE has to sell "choice" in Treasury clearing against netting: the incumbent, FICC, already holds the netting set.

Verdict: this is the clearest link between the two sources. XVA is what P4 costs when you don't clear; the CCP franchises are what P4 earns when a regulator makes clearing mandatory.

Concept 5 · Funding and capital are where the money moved (P5)

The derivatives idea: FVA, MVA and KVA are real costs charged to trades: funding the position, posting initial margin, and holding regulatory capital. When rules raise those costs, activity moves to whoever carries them cheapest.

What the companies show: - JPMorgan has made one argument for six years: capital rules (G-SIB surcharge, SLR, Basel III endgame) treat Treasuries and market-making as riskier than they are. That shrinks dealer balance sheets and pushes intermediation to nonbanks (jpmc capital regulation). In XVA terms, this is a fight over KVA. - Goldman took the other side of the same fact. If balance sheet is scarce, charge for it. Financing grew from 19% of markets revenue (2018) to ~46% (Q3 2026) (goldman markets platforms). - Uncleared trades still need margin. LSEG bought Acadia (margin for uncleared trades: 2,000+ participants, >$1tn of collateral a day) and calls the uncleared market "comparable to" the cleared one (lseg post trade clearing). - The rates layer. wss rates macro and wss trading hedge funds show the same constraint in the basis trade and repo: "the holding period belongs to whoever funds you."

Verdict: this fits strongly, and it's the one most likely to be underrated. P1–P4 are mostly solved and productized. P5 is where pricing power has moved since 2018, for dealers and for margin utilities.

Concept 6 · AI lands on P1 and P6 first, and quant finance supplies the test (P6)

The derivatives idea: ML models are function approximators. In pricing they must respect no-arbitrage, hold up out of sample and survive stress periods. A model that fits the data but breaks those rules is a hidden P2 risk.

What the companies show: the attention map finds that since 2023 all ten firms converged on "AI and tokens" (cross company attention map). The AI products that actually shipped are P1 engines: BVAL's regression-tree ensemble, IBVAL intraday pricing, Tradeweb Ai-Price, ICE's continuous evaluated prices. Tradeweb's "~30% better than the last trade" is the floor test, not a head-to-head with other evaluators (tradeweb ai price).

Verdict: this fits. The derivatives corpus supplies the questions to ask any AI pricing claim: compared with what, out of sample, through a stress period, and does it respect arbitrage bounds? None of the vendors publish that test.

Concept 7 · 2008 created the demand; rules keep creating it

Most of the moats in the matrix trace back to a rule that made one of the six problems mandatory, standard and measurable.

When Rule or event Problem it made mandatory Who it built
2008 Crisis need for "more robust independent pricing" P1 Bloomberg BVAL (bloomberg pricing bval ibval)
2009 CDS clearing pushed by US regulators P4 ICE Clear Credit (ice clearing treasury)
2010s (added context) Dodd-Frank and EMIR clearing and trading mandates; CVA capital charges P3, P4 LCH SwapClear, Tradeweb SEF (tradeweb derivatives regulation)
2016–17 Uncleared margin rules phase in (added context) P5 Acadia, later LSEG (lseg post trade clearing)
2020–23 LIBOR → SOFR P1 Tradeweb's rebooking tools; LCH's discounting switch
2022 SEC Rule 2a-5 (fund fair-value diligence) P1 S&P PVR Source (spglobal pricing fixed income)
2026–27 US Treasury clearing mandate (cash Dec 31 2026, repo Jun 30 2027) P4, P5 ICE's entry ("would not have entered without it"); JPM sponsored clearing (ice clearing treasury, jpmc capital regulation)

Verdict: for this industry, regulation creates demand rather than just limiting it. The pattern predicts the next deals: watch for rules that make a problem mandatory in a market where it is still bilateral or manual.

Where the gaps are: the matrix's four gaps, in six-problem terms

The capability matrix found every stack converging on four gaps. Each one is a six-problem story:

  1. US Treasury clearing (P4 + P5). A new mandate moves counterparty risk and margin into CCPs. The fight is over who holds the netting set.
  2. Private markets data and trading (P1). His post on smoothed private marks says low reported volatility is stale pricing, not low risk. Whoever builds a credible private-markets price owns the P1 position there. That is BlackRock's Preqin bet (blackrock aladdin data).
  3. Tokenized settlement (P5). The pitch is faster collateral movement and less funding tied up in settlement, which is a P5 cost cut, not a new market (jpmc kinexys deposit tokens).
  4. AI products sold to clients (P6 on top of P1). These are only as good as the reference price underneath them (Concept 6).

The derivatives corpus adds three gaps the company studies don't show:

  • XVA compute for mid-size banks (P4–P6). It needs portfolio-wide Monte Carlo, and no firm in the study sells it as a headline product.
  • Corporate hedging transparency (P3). No firm in the study serves the end-user corporate directly.
  • Margin for uncleared trades (P5). Only LSEG/Acadia has a position, and LSEG calls the market as large as the cleared one.

Verdict: where the six-problem lens applies and where it breaks

  • It explains well: why data beats execution on margin (P1); why clearing houses are the deepest moats (P4 netting); why dealers moved into financing (P5); why every stack wants a reference price; and why rules predict deals.
  • It explains weakly: listings, mortgage technology (ICE's Ellie Mae and Black Knight), credit ratings and desktops. Those are distribution and workflow businesses, not risk-transfer ones, and the lens has little to say about them.
  • Bias on both sides: the company notes are mostly each firm's own voice. Rodrigues writes from the dealer's and the system builder's seat. Neither source covers the corporate end-user well.

Retrieval questions

  1. Why does ICE earn ten times more from fixed-income data than from fixed-income trading? Its evaluated price is the P1 ruler: best execution, TCA, indices and its own venue are all graded against it. Execution is a replaceable layer on top of the price.
  2. How is a clearing house related to CVA? CVA is the cost of bilateral counterparty risk (P4). A CCP replaces many bilateral exposures with one netted exposure backed by margin and a shared default fund. Clearing is the institutional substitute for each bank pricing CVA itself.
  3. Why is clearing winner-take-most? Netting cuts both exposure and margin, so a bigger pool is cheaper to clear in, which attracts more trades. That's why ICE must sell "choice" against FICC's existing netting set in Treasuries.
  4. What is Dimon really arguing about, in XVA terms? KVA: the cost of the regulatory capital that trades consume. Higher capital charges make dealers charge more or step back, and the activity moves to nonbanks.
  5. Why did Goldman's financing share of markets revenue more than double? Capital rules made balance sheet scarce (P5), so the dealer charges for it. Its moat moved from execution to financing.
  6. What should you ask about an AI pricing claim like "30% better"? Better than what (last trade is the floor), out of sample, through a stress period, and does it respect no-arbitrage? Those are the P6 tests from quant finance.
  7. Which rule built which moat? BVAL from the 2008 pricing crisis, ICE Clear Credit from 2009 CDS clearing, Tradeweb swaps from trading mandates, S&P PVR Source from Rule 2a-5, ICE's Treasury entry from the 2026–27 clearing mandate.

Open questions to resolve with better data

  • Independent share data for clearing and evaluated pricing. All shares here are self-reported.
  • Head-to-head pricing accuracy (BVAL vs ICE vs CP+ vs Ai-Price), out of sample and through a stress period.
  • XVA vendors (Murex, Numerix, Quaternion and others) are outside the ten studies. A pull on them would test whether XVA compute is a real gap or just one this repo hasn't covered.
  • Corporate treasurers' side of hedging: no source in the repo speaks for them.
